regionName: Central Europe — Fall of the Berlin Wall, 1989

placeFacts.fact: East Berlin was the GDR’s capital from 1949. The Berlin Wall, built on 13 Aug 1961, sealed it from West Berlin until the night of 9 Nov 1989.
Bonn was West Germany’s ‘provisional’ capital from 1949 to 1991—a modest Rhineland city chosen to symbolise democracy’s humble new start after the Nazi era.
Leipzig’s Monday Demonstrations peaked on 9 Oct 1989, when 70,000 marched peacefully, breaking the regime’s will to use force.
Checkpoint Charlie was the most famous crossing between East and West Berlin. Crowds breached it on 9–10 Nov 1989 after Bornholmer Straße opened first at 23:30.
The inner German border ran 1,393 km from the Baltic to Bavaria. Helmstedt guarded the main Autobahn crossing between West Germany and East Germany.
Dresden saw major 1989 protests. Kohl’s speech at the Frauenkirche ruins in Dec 1989 signalled German reunification was imminent.

beatHistory.history: On 9 November 1989, SED spokesman Günter Schabowski announced East Germans could travel freely, effective ‘immediately, without delay’—misreading his briefing notes. Crowds flooded border crossings; Bornholmer Straße opened first at 23:30. Jubilant Berliners began dismantling the Wall that night.

News of the Wall’s opening spread rapidly, and Western governments quickly recognised the changes as irreversible. The GDR had already been haemorrhaging citizens through Hungary and Czechoslovakia since August 1989, when those countries opened their borders. The regime had lost legitimacy before the Wall fell.

East Germans poured into West Germany seeking the Deutschmark and Western goods. On 1 July 1990, monetary union replaced the East Mark at a controversial 1:1 rate for most savings. The move accelerated reunification but caused severe deindustrialisation as East German products became uncompetitive.

NATO membership for a unified Germany was a central issue in international diplomacy. The Two-plus-Four Treaty, signed 12 September 1990, resolved this: unified Germany would remain in NATO, but NATO forces and nuclear weapons would not be deployed on the territory of the former GDR.

Bornholmer Straße border guards, facing tens of thousands and receiving no orders from above, opened the crossing at 23:30 to prevent a dangerous crush. The regime had no contingency for peaceful, mass civil defiance at that scale. Checkpoint Charlie opened minutes later.

West German Chancellor Kohl presented his Ten-Point Plan for reunification on 28 November 1989 without consulting France, Britain, or the United States. East Germany’s first free elections on 18 March 1990 produced a CDU-led government that backed rapid reunification.

France and Britain privately worried about reunified Germany’s power and potential domination of Europe. The Soviet Union initially opposed NATO membership for a unified Germany. Gorbachev ultimately accepted in July 1990 in exchange for German financial assistance and a ban on NATO forces in the former GDR.

Western intelligence agencies struggled to assess whether hardliners in East Germany or the Soviet Union might stage a coup and reverse the democratic changes. Memories of Hungary 1956 and Czechoslovakia 1968 haunted analysts. No military crackdown came; the regime collapsed peacefully from within.

Monetary union on 1 July 1990 halted the mass emigration to West Germany by giving East Germans access to Deutschmarks. Chancellor Kohl promised ‘flourishing landscapes’ in the east, a vision that proved economically painful as deindustrialisation swept the former GDR in the short term.

Germany reunified at midnight on 3 October 1990, when the GDR formally acceded to the Federal Republic. The Two-plus-Four Treaty of 12 September 1990 formally ended Four Power rights over Germany. Berlin was designated the future capital; the government moved there from Bonn in 1999.

fieldBriefs.headline: Schabowski’s mistake opens the Wall
fieldBriefs.fact: Günter Schabowski misread his briefing notes live on TV. Bornholmer Straße opened first at 23:30 on 9 Nov 1989; Checkpoint Charlie followed minutes later.

fieldBriefs.headline: Hungary opens its wire: Aug 1989
fieldBriefs.fact: Hungary opened its Austrian border on 11 Sept 1989; over 13,000 East Germans fled in three days. The inner German border became porous long before the Wall fell.

fieldBriefs.headline: 1:1 exchange: costly but decisive
fieldBriefs.fact: Monetary union on 1 July 1990 set East Marks to Deutschmarks at 1:1. This made East German industry uncompetitive overnight, triggering deindustrialisation.

fieldBriefs.headline: Two-plus-Four: Germany stays in NATO
fieldBriefs.fact: The Two-plus-Four Treaty (12 Sept 1990) ended Four Power rights. Unified Germany stayed in NATO; NATO forces were barred from the former East German territory.

fieldBriefs.headline: Bornholmer first, Charlie second
fieldBriefs.fact: Bornholmer Straße opened first at 23:30 on 9 Nov 1989—not Checkpoint Charlie. Guards, overwhelmed and without orders, opened barriers to prevent a crush.

fieldBriefs.headline: Kohl’s Ten Points: allies blindsided
fieldBriefs.fact: Kohl’s Ten-Point plan (28 Nov 1989) surprised France and Britain. Thatcher and Mitterrand privately feared the consequences of German reunification.

fieldBriefs.headline: Gorbachev’s concession: NATO stays
fieldBriefs.fact: Gorbachev accepted German NATO membership in July 1990. Germany paid billions to fund Soviet troop withdrawal—the price of Gorbachev’s historic concession.

fieldBriefs.headline: No crackdown: lessons of Leipzig
fieldBriefs.fact: After Tiananmen (June 1989), analysts feared an East German crackdown. The SED’s decision not to fire on Leipzig’s marchers on 9 Oct 1989 proved decisive.

fieldBriefs.headline: Kohl’s ‘flourishing landscapes’
fieldBriefs.fact: Kohl promised prosperity in the east. Monetary union (1 July 1990) halted emigration by giving East Germans Deutschmarks—but deindustrialisation followed.

fieldBriefs.headline: 3 October 1990: German Unity Day
fieldBriefs.fact: Germany reunified at midnight 3 Oct 1990, the GDR joining the Federal Republic. Leipzig’s Monday protesters had helped make the regime’s collapse inevitable.
